inline.s: In Hangzhou there was a woman of extremely fierce temper. Whenever she saw ants walking beside the kitchen stove, she would burn them with fire, and no one knows how many ants she destroyed like this. She also often filled up the burrows of earthworms with quicklime. She had just borne a son who was still nursing, when one day she went out on an errand and returned home to find a great black mass upon the bed. In alarm she looked closely, only to discover that it was her own son, who had been bitten to death alive by a huge swarm of ants. The woman was heartbroken, and before long she too suddenly died a sudden death.

In Taicang Prefecture there was a man named Wu Yi. One night he dreamed that two burly men dressed all in green were begging him for help. When Wu Yi awoke he said to himself: “There must be something about to be killed!” When it was light he went out to investigate, and saw several men holding axes and saws, about to fell two ginkgo trees they had just purchased. Only then did Wu Yi understand the dream of the night before. He immediately brought out money and bought the two ginkgo trees, and so those two ginkgo trees were spared from being cut down!

The cruel-hearted, who constantly do evil, bring calamity upon themselves; one should pity them, admonish them, and transform them, so that they can turn from evil to good and transform calamity into blessing. The kind-hearted, who constantly do good, bring blessings upon themselves; one should rejoice for them and praise them, encourage them and help them succeed, so that they may practice good all the more and their blessings be boundless!

Mr. He Longtu said: “When a person first begins to do evil, it is only because of a single mistaken thought at that moment — it is not that he cannot be dissuaded or stopped! Even after he has done evil, there still remains a single thought that his conscience is not yet extinguished, and it is not that he cannot be saved! The world often rejects those who have done evil as if they were enemies; though they wish to wash their hearts and reform and become new persons, because they are not accepted by others, it is hard for them to find the courage to change!”

Everyone wishes to gain the merit of doing good, yet people vainly discriminate and calculate. The more talented only wish the good deeds to be done by themselves, while the more lowly do not wish the good deeds to be done all by others; some even invent falsehoods to wreck the good deeds of others. This only spoils their own state of mind, and does no harm to others at all. Little do they know that if others have good thoughts and good deeds, and I can inspire them, urge them, and praise them, so that they do them more perfectly and more completely, then the good of others is my own good as well — and this is merit without limit!

To go from the common to the holy, the gate of all good is, above all, to rouse the bodhi mind, which is the most excellent and the first. The bodhi mind is like a seed, because it can give rise to all dharmas of goodness. It is like good farmland, because it can cause living beings to grow in goodness. It is like pure water, because it can wash away all the afflictions in the minds of living beings. It is like a blazing great fire, because it can burn away all wrong views. The Nirvana Sutra says: “The Buddha said that cultivating a single good mind can destroy a hundred kinds of evil deeds, just as a very small fire can burn away everything! Know that the myriad good deeds all arise from a single thought of delight in goodness; when the whole virtuous mind is present, then is accomplished our perfect bodhi of eternal joy and the wondrous fruit.”

One night Yu Lingyi caught a thief at his home; the thief turned out to be the son of a neighbor. Yu Lingyi said to him: “It is because poverty has driven you that you have become a thief! I will now give you ten thousand cash as capital to help you earn a living; from now on, never do evil again!” The thief was just leaving with the money when Yu Lingyi called him back and said: “You are a poor man carrying much money home late at night; you may well be questioned by the night patrol. Better that you remain at my house and go home after dawn.” Yu Lingyi never spoke of this matter to anyone for the whole of his life. Later his descendants all passed the imperial examinations in succession; everyone said this was the retribution of one who pitied, admonished, and transformed an evil person.

In the Later Han there was a man named Pang Tong, who whenever he praised the good deeds and good conduct of others always exaggerated beyond the truth. People found this strange and asked him why. Pang Tong replied: “In the present age good people are few and evil people many. To improve the corrupt customs of society and increase one’s own progress in the Way, if I do not praise the good deeds of others to the fullest, then those who wish to do good will be even fewer! When you praise ten people, five may err, but five do not err; and in this way those inclined to do good may all the more spur themselves on — and that suffices!” The instruction of Lord Guan once said: “May heaven forever give birth to good people, may people forever do good deeds, may mouths forever speak good words.” Mr. Pang Tong may be said to have understood this instruction well and to have practiced it himself; he is truly of benefit to the world and to the human heart!

When one meets the urgent needs of others — as in sickness the urgent need of medicine, in death the urgent need of burial, in hunger and cold the urgent need of clothing and food, and so forth — we should generously open our purses and give help in time to meet the urgent need. When one meets the calamities of others — such as floods, fires, accidents, the ruin of families, and the like — we should, according to our own strength, go to rescue and remove their perils, so that they may turn danger into safety.

When others meet with calamity and distress, if one can make good use of a single word to rescue them, this merit can, above, benefit one’s ancestors, and, below, bring blessings to one’s children and grandchildren. Know that the same hand that pushes a person down also lifts him up! The same mouth that harms others also praises them! Therefore one would rather use the hand that lifts than open the mouth that harms. If one can act accordingly, one need not ask about the future — the future will surely be good!

The Record of Auspicious Blessings says: “Whenever one saves a life, the expense to oneself is not great; only those well-fed and well-clothed, who do not know the suffering of hunger and cold, think it of no account and pay no attention. When the faces of the starving turn sallow and green, one neither heeds nor cares; when the starving are gravely ill and in danger, one thinks it now hopeless to save them, and so watches them die before one’s eyes. Even if a well-meaning person passes by and sees, he can only heave a sigh of sympathy; while the other passers-by look askance, unconcerned, and keep far away.”

Know that a hungry person easily falls ill; once ill he has no strength to beg, and so the more he hungers the deeper and more serious it grows. Thus the earlier the starving are rescued the better. At the very start, only three or four liters of grain are enough to restore their strength and vitality. For a rich man, the cost of a single night’s lodging is enough to save ten lives! If the strength of many is gathered together, it is done even more easily. For instance, one may set up an empty room, pile up straw or warm clothing in it, and take in these poor, sick, cold and hungry people, so that they need not endure in the open the suffering of wind and dew and sleeping out of doors; in this way they can more easily nurse their bodies and recover their health, especially in cold weather, where the need is most urgent! Such measures for rescue can prevent many of the starving from falling ill or dying. For when a person falls ill and no one pays heed, one added disease comes upon him; if he still stays outside and is drenched by the rain, a second disease is added; with the added fear and anxiety, a third disease; and with an empty stomach and nothing to eat, filthy clothing, and wandering and dragging on, how can there be any hope of living! Therefore we should put ourselves in their place and think for them: all are human; if we, like them, met with calamity, we should be just as they are now! Today, happily lacking neither food nor clothing, one wishes instead to increase one’s own pleasures, hoping to store up more wealth for one’s descendants to enjoy; and yet before the pressing good deed of saving those before him, he parts with no coin at all. Little does he know that flood, fire, thieves, sickness, and calamity — these can all sweep his family wealth away! Know that the blessings we now enjoy were formed by doing good and giving in past lives, and are by no means amassed through meanness and stingy scrimping! Once impermanence arrives, when the eyes close and the legs stretch out, nothing can be carried away; what wealth is left becomes only the means of descendants’ wine, women, and gambling! Better to accumulate virtue and leave a blessing to posterity — this is truly a reasonable man! To regard money as one’s life and refuse to part with a single coin is truly to be without a mind and without wisdom!

In the Song dynasty, Wang Zeng, on his way to the capital for the examinations, heard a mother and daughter weeping by the roadside, their weeping most grievous. Wang Zeng asked a neighbor in the area, who said: “This mother and daughter are poor and have fallen into arrears with the public treasury, and the officials press them hard; so they are about to sell the daughter to repay the debt — that is why they weep.” Wang Zeng then went to visit their home and found it was truly so. Wang Zeng said to the mother: “You may sell the daughter to me. Because I hold office, I must often pass through this place, and so mother and daughter may see one another often.” Thereupon he gave her the amount of money she owed the treasury, and agreed that after three days he would take the daughter away. But after three days, Wang Zeng did not come to take the daughter. The mother found it strange and went to the place where Wang Zeng was staying; but Wang Zeng had already departed, and had left behind a letter telling the mother to choose a faithful and dependable family for her daughter to be married into. Later, when Wang Zeng went to the capital for the examinations, he was ranked first three times in succession, attained a very high office, and was even enfeoffed by the emperor as the Duke of Yi.

In the place called Xinjian there had once been a great famine. A certain family was reduced to the utmost poverty, leaving only a little more than a liter of grain. So they cooked rice and put poison in it, intending to eat their fill together and then die. Just as they were about to eat, the village headman happened to arrive to press them for the arrears they owed the public treasury; seeing their cooked rice, he wanted to eat it. The poor man hurriedly stopped him, saying: “This rice is not what you should eat!” and then tearfully told him the reason. The headman was grieved on hearing it, and said to him: “How can your family have come to such poverty! Though my family also lacks grain, we still have five pecks of rice. Let it be so — come home with me and take some rice, and at least you can eat for a few more days!” When the poor man carried the rice home, he discovered fifty taels of gold inside the rice bag. Thinking this must be public money, he hurriedly took it back to return it to the headman. The headman said: “This is not the government’s money; it must be heaven’s gift to us!” So they divided the gold equally, and both families were able to pass through the famine year in safety.

The man Duan Nianba had grain stored in dozens of granaries. When a famine year came, he wished to seize the chance to reap a windfall, and so raised the price of the grain to sell it. The authorities sent a man to Duan Nianba’s home to borrow grain for famine relief, and Duan Nianba agreed. But the next morning, on seeing a great crowd of starving people lined up outside his gate waiting for grain, Duan Nianba repented and would not give out the grain. The starving people then set up an uproar. Duan Nianba ordered his household to shut all the doors and turn everyone away. Just at that moment, suddenly the weather changed: great wind and rain, thunder and lightning, came together. Strange to say, the grain in the Duan family granaries all piled up, heap upon heap, out in the street. When the starving people saw it, they all hastened to seize it, and within less than a moment they had taken all the grain away; while Duan Nianba was struck dead by the thunder.
Supplementary Note

When a famine year comes, those who live near the mountains may gather pine and cypress to relieve hunger. The Records of Natural Studies says: “In a famine year, with nothing to eat, one may pound pine and cypress; the juice that is pressed out, taken together with boiling water, may be drunk until one is merely not hungry. Using the clear congee broth to take the pine and cypress juice is even better. Each time use five measures of pine juice and three measures of cypress juice, ground and taken; or one may use pine leaves alone, which is also fine; but one must abstain from all food, and then it will naturally have the effect of relieving hunger and curing illness.”

In Gaoyou there was a man called Zhang Baihu. Once, sitting in a boat, he saw a person far off clinging to the overturned hull of a boat, bobbing up and down in the utmost danger, crying loudly for help. Zhang Baihu called out, asking the fishing boats to go to his rescue, but none of the boats responded. Zhang immediately took out ten taels of silver and gave them to the boatman, who then consented to go to the rescue. Having saved the man, this one who was nearly drowned turned out to be none other than Zhang Baihu’s own son!

When one sees others fortunate and elated, one should feel as if it were one’s own fortune, and moreover do one’s utmost to support them; when one sees others unfortunate and dejected, one should feel as if it were one’s own misfortune, and should go to their rescue in every way.

People today, when they see the gain and loss of others, cannot take them as their own gain and loss. The reason is nothing but a single heart set on themselves. Hoping to gain and fearing to lose, they then give rise to the thought of fearing that others may gain and preferring to let others lose. At first it is only for one’s own profit, but gradually it comes to the point of harming others. Yet to envy the success of others and delight in their failure is in fact quite unrelated to success or failure in human affairs; it only spoils one’s own state of mind and plants the seed of evil, and in the end brings harm to oneself. Little do we know that the work of sages and saints is originally to eliminate the view of self, and that the insight of the enlightened must also break through vulgar feelings. If one realizes that self and others are originally one, and that gain and loss are all determined by heaven, then seeing the gain of others, one not only does not envy it but extends every kind of support and assistance; seeing the loss of others, one not only does not rejoice but gives every kind of rescue and protection — this is the true benefit for oneself!
Story:

When Xue Yuan was prime minister of the state of Yan, he could not treat people and handle affairs with an impartial heart, but envied what others gained and delighted in what others lost; he would not recommend worthy and able persons to Yan, but was envious of them and obstructed them, so that they could not be of use to the king of Yan. As a result, one of Xue Yuan’s sons died in prison, and all his other sons became cripples. Gongming Zigao then transmitted the Zhong Jing Jing (Sutra of the Middle Admonitions) to Xue Yuan; after reading the sutra and hearing the Dharma, Xue Yuan deeply regretted his past conduct, and made a vow to uphold and practice the teachings of the Zhong Jing Jing. In the end he preserved only a single child.
Fine Words:

Master Lianchi of the Ming dynasty once said: “As for people’s response to the temptations of wealth, sex, fame, and profit in this world, each person’s power of concentration in resisting such temptations differs greatly; now I will use a metaphor to explain it. Suppose here is a pile of fire, and beside the fire are set five different substances. The first is like dry grass: as soon as it touches the fire, it burns. The second is like wood: with only a breath of wind upon it, it too catches fire and burns. The third is like iron: it will not burn, but once the fire burns long enough it melts. The fourth is like water: not only does it refuse to burn, it even puts out the fire; but if the water is placed in a pot and heated, it is still brought to a boil by the fire! The fifth is like empty space: know that in empty space there is nothing to burn; however the fire may burn, it remains as still and unmoved as empty space! And as the fire burns on and on, after it has burned long enough it goes out of itself!” So those who would make the mind impartial should contemplate in this way.
Do not publicize the faults of others; rather, one should earnestly conceal them for him. Do not vaunt your own strengths; rather, keep them hidden and nurture your virtue.

When one hears or sees the faults of others, it is like hearing the names of one’s parents: the ears may hear them, but the mouth cannot speak them. Yet while the mouth surely cannot speak them, if the ears also would not hear them, would that not be even better! For who has no faults? If one publicizes the faults of others, the word inevitably spreads abroad, lessening their reputation and corrupting their conduct — for whose sin is this to answer! Unless one is an utterly unscrupulous scoundrel, one surely would not do such a thing.

One’s own virtues and strengths should be like those of a wise merchant, who keeps his wealth deeply hidden and does not reveal it; if the wealth is revealed, there is danger! In this life, every person surely has his strengths and merits; the most important thing is to know how to keep them veiled and nurture virtue, day by day renewing, and only then can one’s own character be accomplished. Laozi said: “Those who possess great virtue often appear, in their countenance, to look dull and foolish.” Zisi also said in the Doctrine of the Mean: “The gentleman’s way of conduct is to show nothing outwardly while the beauty is within; in time it naturally becomes evident day by day.” These teachers’ instructions are so clear and plain; therefore we should all carefully reflect on them!

In the Spring and Autumn period, King Zhuang of Chu one evening invited his ministers to a banquet. In the midst of the banquet the candles suddenly went out. A minister, drunk, took advantage of the darkness and tugged at the clothing of the king’s beloved consort, taking the opportunity to make advances. The consort at once tore off the minister’s hatband as evidence, and reported it to King Zhuang. On hearing this, King Zhuang said: “My purpose in feasting my ministers is that they all may drink to the full. Now one of them, drunk, has committed a fault. If, in order to make prominent my consort’s chastity, I would expose a minister’s fault, this is a thing I will never do!” So King Zhuang ordered his attendants not to light the candles, and sent word: “He who drinks with me — if he does not tear off his own hatband, it shows he has not enjoyed himself this evening!” When the ministers heard this, they all tore off their hatbands, and the banquet ended in great joy. Later, when King Zhuang fought with the army of Jin, he was closely besieged by the Jin forces; the battle was fierce and the situation most perilous. Then King Zhuang saw a warrior who, unafraid of death, fought his way forward against the Jin army, and by doing so freed the king from the crisis of being surrounded. When King Zhuang asked about him, he learned that this warrior was Jiang Xiong — the very minister whose hatband had been torn off by the consort that night while he was drunk!

Mr. Zhang Gongchen said: “Do not lightly discard the good of others; do not lightly believe the words of others; do not lightly follow the pleasure of others; do not lightly speak of the faults of others.” These are the ways of holding oneself in loyalty and generosity; and to reveal the faults of others is especially the very root of cruelty and treachery.

In the Song dynasty, Ouyang Xiu wrote extremely well and was a famous great writer in history; yet in receiving guests he always spoke much of the affairs of state administration and never spoke of literature. Cai Xiang, on the other hand, was expert in government affairs, yet in receiving guests he spoke much of literature and never of politics. Both gentlemen were excellent at keeping themselves veiled, and did not parade their strengths before others; therefore in history both enjoyed great renown, and they both rose to offices of the utmost eminence.

In the Yongchun era of the Tang dynasty, Lu Zhaolin, Luo Binwang, Wang Bo, and Yang Jiong — the four famous literati, known in history as the Four Outstanding Figures of the Early Tang — all enjoyed great renown for their writings. People at the time considered the four to have talent surpassing the age, and that, being young, they must surely reach the most exalted positions in future official life. But when Pei Xingjian saw the four, he said: “If a scholar is to prosper far and make great plans, one should first look to see whether he has a broad and generous capacity of character, and only afterwards at his writing! As for the four like Wang Bo, though their writing is good, they are in general hasty and shallow, fond of showing off their talent — this is not the stock that enjoys rank and fortune! Yang Jiong is a little the more calm and reserved; for him to come to a good end would be extremely fortunate!” Later the fates of the four indeed matched Pei Xingjian’s words. Lu Zhaolin, Wang Bo, and Luo Binwang all died young; only Yang Jiong lived the longer.

So from these facts one can see that ability is not equal to learning, vigor is not equal to virtue and capacity, and writing is not equal to conduct. People of old long ago clearly set forth this principle; therefore to show off one’s strengths is something a gentleman does not do! Especially the people of today, who often keep the phrase “worthy of pride” on their lips, and everyone hearing it takes it as a matter of course and does not regard it as wrong. Know that fullness attracts loss while modesty gains benefit; only the humble can truly enjoy blessings!

We should check people from doing evil, lest they gradually run wild and others come to be harmed by them; and, further, we should praise the good conduct of others, so that they may practice good without weariness and others also be guided by them.

As for a person’s doing evil, it is not caused by his original nature! But if a person is accustomed to doing evil and has been soiled too deeply, then he is hard to save. Whether one knowingly does wrong, or unknowingly acts in error, in the end one commits a sin that covers heaven. Trace it back to its beginning, and it is but a single mistaken thought at the start! Yet everyone has a conscience. When he first begins to err and the evil thought has just arisen, one should with earnest, kind words admonish him and remind him, and even do one’s utmost to stop him. Who has no heart? After such admonition and reminder, how could he fail to turn from evil to good? Even if, unhappily, one has already committed great evil, if I can reach him with perfect sincerity and curb him and stop him, then his good mind may well arise, and he may resolutely wash his heart, reform himself, and repent and wash away the evil karma he has committed! Moreover, people are not sages; how could they do good in everything! If he has but a single word or deed that is worthy, one should immediately praise him and commend him. This can make those already doing good firm in their resolve and the more diligent in doing good; and those not yet doing good, hearing of it, will also give rise to admiration and the resolve to emulate — is this not to obey heaven’s command?

The Daoists say: “Curb evil and promote good.” The Buddhists say: “Stop evil and practice good.” The Confucians say: “Conceal evil and promote good.” The doctrines of the three teachings seem to come from a single mouth. From this we know that the sage’s mind-substance is empty, spiritual, and clear to the very depths, and that not even the slightest trace of desire is retained! It is like a bright mirror reflecting things: as it is shone upon, so it manifests; and as it manifests, so it transforms away. Thus when the sage sees evil, he can naturally dissolve it; when he sees good, he can bring it to great brightness. Therefore the sage curbs evil and promotes good, solely in order to restore and complete the nature that living beings originally possess!

As the Four Teachings of Liaofan relates, before the great Shun became ruler, by the shore of Leize Lake he saw strong young fishermen all taking the deep places of the water to catch fish, while the old and weak fished where the current ran swift and the water was shallow. The strong young fishermen had taken for themselves all the good places. Seeing this, Shun grieved and pitied them. He thought of a method: he himself also went to catch fish; on seeing those who delighted in seizing, he covered over their faults and did not say anything of them; on seeing the more yielding fishermen, he praised them everywhere, took them as a model, and imitated their way of yielding. Thus, after Shun had fished for a year, everyone yielded the deep places, where fish were plentiful, to others. The story of Shun is only used to exhort people; one must not misunderstand it as urging people to catch fish. Know that catching fish is the sin of taking life, and must never be done. Then how is it that Shun, so clear and intelligent, could not have spoken a few pertinent words to teach the multitudes, and had to take part himself? Understand that Shun did not teach the people with words, but made himself the example, so that people on seeing it felt ashamed and changed their selfish minds — this is the careful effort of a person of deep purpose!

Curb your own evil, then you can curb the evil of others; promote the good of others, then you can urge others to do good.’ This means: first be able to curb your own evil, and then you can curb the evil of others; first be able to praise the good of others, and then you can urge others to practice good!

Whether brothers divide their property, or friends pass money between them, one should yield and make concession, giving the larger portion to the brother or friend and taking for oneself the smaller portion; let others have the advantage, while one is willing to take the loss.

Between brothers there is the bond of flesh and blood and the natural relationship of heaven, while wealth is a thing outside the body, and so one should surely yield! The Buddha said in the Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching: “Those of great desire, because they greedily seek after benefit, have more suffering and affliction than others; those of few desires, having nothing they seek and no greed, have not so much suffering and affliction. If a person wishes to free himself from all the various sufferings and afflictions, he should understand contentment; and the way of contentment is the most secure abode of wealth, honor, and happiness! The contented, even lying on the ground, are at ease and joyful; the discontented, even dwelling in heaven, are not contented and not joyful!” From this we know that if a person can, in matters of wealth, yield the more and take the less, his mind is naturally at peace; no external state can disturb it, and so he forever knows contentment and joy!

Mr. Yu Tieqiao said: “Wealth is the vital breath of heaven and earth. A person in this world, without wealth, cannot survive; and there is no one under heaven who does not love wealth, and no day in which wealth is not used! Therefore wealth is an indispensable necessity of life. Yet the amount of wealth allotted to each person is fixed; to wish for more is impossible! However, each person’s habits in spending wealth are very different, and each has his bias: the prodigal flings away a thousand gold at a throw; the miser will not part with a single coin; the incorruptible, when a man sends him money at night, refuses it and will not accept; the greedy and tyrannical, even in broad daylight, will dare openly to rob and steal! Know that the miser’s insight is shallow and narrow, and he treasures each coin and cent as a precious thing; just as a bee protects the honey it has made, and a child protects the cake he hides in his breast, unwilling to share the least part with others. Yet this is still to keep what is his allotted share; it is merely annoying, and heaven does not on that account rage against his stinginess. But the greedy and tyrannical seek wealth that is not their allotted share, and are insatiable in greed; like a fish swallowing a boat, or a snake swallowing an elephant, in their greediness! Brothers quarreling, friends making enemies, robbers killing men, corrupt officials perverting the law, treacherous ministers betraying the state — all are produced by this single thought of greed! Therefore Taishang has in this chapter again and again set forth the calamity of coveting wealth. Yet to teach men not to wrongfully take wealth is right; if one were to teach men to take no wealth at all, that indeed would not do. So Taishang here gives the two words ‘more’ and ‘less’, enabling people to proportion themselves accordingly, as the proper way of taking wealth. And the measure of more and less has no fixed standard: for a poor man, one tael of gold is no small sum! For a rich man, ten thousand taels of gold are no great store! The incorruptible, who should receive a hundred coins but receives ten, does not feel it little; the greedy, who should receive a hundred coins but receives a thousand, does not feel it much. Only the man of impartial mind measures the amount he should receive, and in taking does not exceed his due portion — this is the method of taking less. Yet the human heart always fears having little and hopes for more, and this too is the common feeling of people. But if one can accord with conditions and not strive, then one naturally will not do evil; if one insists on always seeing more and withdrawing from it, would that not be to run counter to common feeling? Alas! Know that the coming of wealth has many different causes and conditions. The wealth we may take before our eyes is not necessarily what is allotted in our destiny; but in the hidden realm, all the number allotted to me I have no power to know, and no way to examine. If by any chance I take wealth that is not in my destiny, it is like taking poisoned wine and rotten meat to eat — can one eat it in peace and fullness? So better to withdraw from it, and that is the surer course! If I withdraw wealth that is not in my destiny, I can surely avoid my own fault; even if I mistakenly withdraw wealth that is in my destiny, then that withdrawn wealth will certainly come again from some other quarter! Faced with wealth, one must hold out and endure, and not let the eyes open at the sight of money and act carelessly! For the rich this is easier; for the poor it is far harder. If, knowing the difficulty, one still labors earnestly to do it, so that ghosts and spirits perceive this heart that dares not be in the least careless, then although one lives in the depth of poverty and hardship, one will not come to the point of being unable to go on living. If one can believe these principles truly and hold to them steadfastly, then the way of taking less is the way of becoming rich!”

In the Song dynasty there was a man named Xu Ji, who divided property with his second uncle. He first asked his second uncle to take all he wanted, and then he would take what was left. When the second uncle had finished taking, only a case of books and two run-down old rooms remained; Xu Ji accepted them with composure, and felt in his heart not the slightest resentment or regret!
